Home‑improvement retailers are interested in stocking safety products for emergency preparedness.
predictions: Sales of 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in regions with high household emergency preparedness activity.
Retailers will allocate shelf space to the product if it demonstrates safety effectiveness.
Consumer price sensitivity will be moderate, allowing premium pricing for a differentiated model.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Outdoor Enthusiasts vs Household Emergency Preparedness
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and 100 household emergency preparedness buyers (homeowners, preppers). Each respondent is shown a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon (same as in sources) and a price of €350. They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself?" (binary yes/no). The survey also collects demographic data (age, gender, region).
X1.sample: 200 respondents (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 household emergency preparedness buyers)
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents who say "yes" to purchasing the device)

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than household emergency preparedness buyers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Household emergency preparedness buyers will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than outdoor enthusiasts.

X1.decision_rule: If the purchase intent rate for outdoor enthusiasts is at least 10 percentage points higher than for household emergency preparedness buyers, we conclude T1 is better supported. If household buyers are at least 10 percentage points higher, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or actual purchase behavior for outdoor enthusiasts or household emergency preparedness buyers. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure actual purchase intent among outdoor enthusiasts versus household emergency preparedness buyers. If the test shows outdoor enthusiasts have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than household buyers, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer product for the
final.target_customer: Outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) who need a reliable distress beacon for remote environments.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that is easy to use, durable, and marketed as a safety device for outdoor recreation, sold through outdoor retailers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) with 200 respondents (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 household emergency preparedness buyers) to measure purchase intent rates.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to regulatory descriptions and anecdotal rescues; actual consumer demand, willingness to pay, and market size are unknown. The test will resolve uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows household buyers have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than outdoor enthusiasts, we would shift focus to the household market.
If both groups show similar intent, we would maintain the current strategic pause and consider other options.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.

Evidence must address consumer demand, market viability, and ACR’s ability to capture value.
Any recommendation must be grounded in observable data, not assumptions or later developments.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., personal distress beacon for outdoor enthusiasts) using the 406 MHz technology.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, market viability, and ACR’s ability to capture value.
Any recommendation must be grounded in observable data, not assumptions or later developments.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., personal distress beacon for outdoor enthusiasts) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand into consumer market without differentiation (e.g., sell existing beacons directly to individual buyers).
3) No expansion – continue focusing on B2B/military/marine customers.
4) Pursue a different route to market (e.g., partner with outdoor retailers) or target a different customer segment (e.g., emergency preparedness kits for households).

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Outdoor Enthusiasts vs Household Emergency Preparedness
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and 100 household emergency preparedness buyers (homeowners, preppers). Each respondent is shown a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon (same as in sources) and a price of €350. They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself?" (binary yes/no). The survey also collects demographic data (age, gender, region).
X1.sample: 200 respondents (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 household emergency preparedness buyers)
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents who say "yes" to purchasing the device)

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than household emergency preparedness buyers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Household emergency preparedness buyers will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than outdoor enthusiasts.

X1.decision_rule: If the purchase intent rate for outdoor enthusiasts is at least 10 percentage points higher than for household emergency preparedness buyers, we conclude T1 is better supported. If household buyers are at least 10 percentage points higher, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or actual purchase behavior for outdoor enthusiasts or household emergency preparedness buyers. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure actual purchase intent among outdoor enthusiasts versus household emergency preparedness buyers. If the test shows outdoor enthusiasts have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than household buyers, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer product for the
final.target_customer: Outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) who need a reliable distress beacon for remote environments.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that is easy to use, durable, and marketed as a safety device for outdoor recreation, sold through outdoor retailers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) with 200 respondents (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 household emergency preparedness buyers) to measure purchase intent rates.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to regulatory descriptions and anecdotal rescues; actual consumer demand, willingness to pay, and market size are unknown. The test will resolve uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows household buyers have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than outdoor enthusiasts, we would shift focus to the household market.
If both groups show similar intent, we would maintain the current strategic pause and consider other options.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, and identify the key evidence that would support this decision.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; cannot use later developments.

Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, residential lawn care, or a niche industrial application).

X1.name: Deere Premium vs Standard Dealer Pricing Test
X1.method: Survey individual homeowners in a region with active Deere dealers. Randomly assign them to one of two groups: Group A receives a standard Deere lawn and garden tractor (e.g., a basic model) offered at the dealer’s standard price. Group B receives the same tractor but with premium features (e.g., comfort, ergonomic design, additional attachments) offered at a 20% higher price. Both groups are shown the same product information and have the same opportunity to ask questions. After a week, collect willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) data (maximum price they would pay) and purchase intent (binary).
X1.sample: 300 homeowners in a region where Deere dealers are active, recruited via local community boards and online forums. Ensure at least 150 per group.
X1.measure: WTP (maximum price) and purchase intent (binary) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than Group B because consumers value durability and reliability over premium features.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than Group A because consumers are willing to pay a premium for comfort and ease of use.

X1.decision_rule: If Group B’s average WTP is at least 15% higher than Group A’s, conclude T2 is more likely. If Group A’s average WTP is at least 15% higher, conclude T1 is more likely. If the difference is less than 15%, both theories remain uncertain.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25‑65 who own a small garden (under 1/4 acre). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of a consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor priced at $1,200 (approximately 1962‑era cost). Group B receives the same description but also emphasizes prestige and status signaling (e.g., "a tractor that shows your home’s value and your commitment to quality"). Both groups are told the tractor is available through a local dealer and can be financed. After reading the description, participants are asked: "Would you be interested in purchasing this tractor?" (binary response).
X1.sample: 500 homeowners (250 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who indicate "Yes" to purchasing).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B because affordability and practicality are the primary drivers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A because prestige and status signaling are the primary drivers.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent rate is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B, T1 is supported. If Group B’s purchase intent rate is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, neither theory is supported.

arguments.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25‑65 who own a small garden (under 1/4 acre). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of a consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor priced at $1,200 (approximately 1962‑era cost). Group B receives the same description but also emphasizes prestige and status signaling (e.g., "a tractor that shows your home’s value and your commitment to quality"). Both groups are told the tractor is available through a local dealer and can be financed. After reading the description, participants are asked: "Would you be interested in purchasing this tractor?" (binary response).
arguments.sample: 500 homeowners (250 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who indicate "Yes" to purchasing).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B because affordability and practicality are the primary drivers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A because prestige and status signaling are the primary drivers.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent rate is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B, T1 is supported. If Group B’s purchase intent rate is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, neither theory is supported.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey (Test X1) to measure purchase intent under affordability versus prestige messaging. If the survey shows a 10‑point difference in favor of affordability, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on affordability and practicality. X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions: one emphasizing affordability and practicality for small gardens, and one emphasizing prestige and status. Participants are recruited from households with small gardens (under 0.5 acres) in the U.S. They are asked to indicate their primary reason for purchasing a lawn and garden tractor (e.g., affordability, status, or other).
X1.sample: 500 households with small gardens, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Primary purchase motivation (affordability vs. status) measured on a 1‑7 Likert scale (1 = affordability, 7 = status). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) for each product variant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to the affordability description will report affordability as their primary reason (average score ≥ 4) and will show higher WTP for the affordability variant.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to the prestige description will report status as their primary reason (average score ≥ 4) and will show higher WTP for the prestige variant.

X1.decision_rule: If the average primary motivation score for the affordability variant is at least 4 and at least 1.5 points higher than the prestige variant, T1 is supported. If the prestige variant score is at least 4 and at least 1.5 points higher, T2 is supported. If neither variant meets the threshold, both theories remain uncertain.

final.value_proposition: A lawn and garden tractor priced at a level comparable to existing competitive brands, leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network to reach consumers directly.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Survey (X1) within the €15,000 budget and 12‑week timeline.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to a single independent study showing a 76‑percent sales growth for lawn and garden equipment from 1960 to 1979. There is no direct evidence that consumers purchase tractors for affordability versus prestige. A
would_change_if: If the survey shows prestige as the primary driver with a threshold of at least 4 and a 1.5‑point advantage over affordability, we would shift focus to a prestige‑driven proposition.
If the survey shows neither driver meets the threshold, we would remain uncertain and consider other options such as licensing or expanding the existing dealer network.

X1.name: Homeowner Survey: Price vs. Versatility vs. Status
X1.method: Online survey of 500 U.S. homeowners aged 35‑65, recruited via a panel in Q3 2022. Participants are shown a description of a Deere lawn and garden tractor (model X) with three options: (A) basic model priced at $1,500, (B) versatile model priced at $2,000 (can be used for farm and garden), and (C) status model priced at $2,500 (branded as premium, emphasizes Deere’s tractor heritage). They are asked to indicate which option they would purchase and the primary reason (price, versatility, status).
X1.sample: 500 homeowners, balanced by age, gender, and geographic region to reflect 1962 U.S. household demographics.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (percentage selecting each option) and primary reason (price, versatility, status) for each option.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent for the versatile model (option B) than for the basic model (option A), because small‑holder farmers would value a single tool for both farm and garden work.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent for the status model (option C) than for the basic model (option A), because homeowners would pay a premium for a brand associated with quality and innovation, even if the machine serves only residential garden tasks.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants selecting the versatile model (option B) is at least 15 percentage points higher than the proportion selecting the basic model (option A), conclude T1 is supported. If the proportion selecting the status model (option C) is at least 15 percentage points higher than the proportion selecting the basic model (option A), conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

arguments.claim: Small‑holder farmers will adopt Deere lawn and garden tractors if they perceive them as affordable, versatile tools for multiple tasks, because they already use tractors for farming and want a single machine that can also serve residential garden needs.
arguments.who_benefits: Deere and individual buyers (small‑holders and homeowners) who need a multi‑purpose machine.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If a tractor can be repurposed for both farm and garden work, buyers reduce the need to buy multiple machines, increasing adoption.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling a single tractor that serves two markets, potentially higher margins from one design versus two distinct products.
assumptions: Small‑holder farmers already own tractors suitable for farming.
Garden tractors must be capable of tasks such as tilling, plowing, or mowing small yards.
Cost sensitivity is a primary driver for small‑holders.
predictions: If a survey of small‑holder farmers shows willingness to pay a premium for a versatile machine, the theory will be supported.
Sales of a single‑purpose lawn tractor will be lower than a multi‑purpose model.

arguments.claim: Homeowners will adopt Deere lawn and garden tractors because they perceive them as a status symbol and a sign of modern living, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand associated with quality and innovation, even if the machine serves only residential garden tasks.
arguments.who_benefits: Deere and individual buyers (homeowners) who value brand prestige and are willing to pay more for a premium product.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Status-driven buyers are motivated by the social signal of owning a well-known brand, and are willing to allocate budget to a product that signals sophistication and modernity.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling a premium-priced product that leverages brand equity, potentially higher margins and brand loyalty.
assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 are aware of Deere as a tractor manufacturer and associate it with quality.
Status and brand perception are significant drivers of purchase decisions for residential lawn equipment.
Price sensitivity is secondary to brand prestige for this segment.
predictions: If a survey of homeowners shows willingness to pay a premium for a Deere lawn tractor, the theory will be supported.
Sales of a premium-priced lawn tractor will be higher than a basic model priced at the same cost.

arguments.name: Homeowner Survey: Price vs. Versatility vs. Status
arguments.method: Online survey of 500 U.S. homeowners aged 35‑65, recruited via a panel in Q3 2022. Participants are shown a description of a Deere lawn and garden tractor (model X) with three options: (A) basic model priced at $1,500, (B) versatile model priced at $2,000 (can be used for farm and garden), and (C) status model priced at $2,500 (branded as premium, emphasizes Deere’s tractor heritage). They are asked to indicate which option they would purchase and the primary reason (price, versatility, status).
arguments.sample: 500 homeowners, balanced by age, gender, and geographic region to reflect 1962 U.S. household demographics.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (percentage selecting each option) and primary reason (price, versatility, status) for each option.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent for the versatile model (option B) than for the basic model (option A), because small‑holder farmers would value a single tool for both farm and garden work.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent for the status model (option C) than for the basic model (option A), because homeowners would pay a premium for a brand associated with quality and innovation, even if the machine serves only residential garden tasks.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants selecting the versatile model (option B) is at least 15 percentage points higher than the proportion selecting the basic model (option A), conclude T1 is supported. If the proportion selecting the status model (option C) is at least 15 percentage points higher than the proportion selecting the basic model (option A), conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.
